comparison: Both evaluate methodology claims (C21-C26, C33-C40) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval focuses on comprehensive documentation of expert recruitment and interview procedures. Peer review praises the consistent methodology for eliciting predictions. OpenEval also covers modeling methodology (C27-C31) and evaluation (C32) which peer review includes in the same result, showing broader grouping by peer reviewers.

OpenEval evaluates modeling methodology claims (C27-C31) as SUPPORTED with focus on mathematical framework and technical specifications. Peer review includes these same claims in their broader methodology evaluation (R1), treating them as part of the overall study design without separate technical assessment.

OpenEval evaluates evaluation methodology (C32, Brier score) as SUPPORTED but notes additional metrics could strengthen analysis. Peer review includes C32 in their overall methodology assessment without specific comment on the scoring approach or suggesting additional metrics.

Perfect agreement on forecast results (C41-C48). Both evaluate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes specific quantitative probabilities and concrete examples of successes/failures. Peer review treats these as factual observations accepted without challenge, summarizing the key finding about comparable performance.

Perfect agreement on performance comparisons (C49-C54). Both evaluate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the evaluation is limited to one metric (Brier score) and emphasizes the finding about no consistent expert outperformance. Peer review affirms these findings without methodological concerns, with editor stating evidence is convincing.

Perfect agreement on systematic bias findings (C55-C58). Both evaluate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the compelling evidence of 12/15 experts showing the same over-cautious bias pattern. Peer review accepts these findings without challenge, implicitly acknowledging the systematic nature in their discussion of forecast patterns.

Perfect agreement on flare-up prediction findings (C59-C64). Both evaluate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes experts had limited success and that including models worsened ensemble performance. Peer review explicitly affirms this as a key result, stating 'experts consistently outperformed the models' in predicting new outbreak locations.

Both address comparative findings (C65-C68) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval also includes interpretation claims (C69-C70) in separate result R9. Peer review groups C65-C72 together, encompassing both the comparative results and their interpretation, treating the threshold-dependent performance pattern as part of the overall comparative analysis.

OpenEval evaluates interpretation of threshold-dependent performance (C69-C70) as SUPPORTED but notes alternative explanations could be considered. Peer review includes these claims in their broader comparative analysis (R6) as SUPPORTED without raising concerns about the interpretation or suggesting alternatives.

OpenEval evaluates ensemble justification (C71-C72) as SUPPORTED, emphasizing that no individual expert consistently outperformed the ensemble. Peer review includes these claims in their broader comparative performance evaluation (R6) as SUPPORTED, affirming that 'no expert's predictions were consistently better than the others.'

Significant disagreement on novelty claims (C74-C75). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting the claim is plausible but lacks comprehensive verification through systematic review. Peer review rates as SUPPORTED, implicitly accepting novelty with statements about the analysis being 'important and unique' and providing quantification 'rarely' done before.

Disagreement on methodological limitations (C76-C81). OpenEval evaluates as SUPPORTED, treating these as appropriately stated valid concerns. Peer review rates as UNCERTAIN, raising additional concerns about applicability to early outbreak stages and emphasizing the need to replicate such studies, suggesting the limitations may be more significant than acknowledged.

Both evaluate model utility arguments (C82-C85, C87) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the conclusion depends on specific models and outbreak phase studied. Peer review affirms these conclusions more strongly, stating the research has 'important implications' and evidence is 'convincing,' with one reviewer commending it as 'an interesting and important contribution.'

OpenEval evaluates combination approach suggestions (C88, C94) as UNCERTAIN, noting limited concrete guidance and that C64 shows including models reduced flare-up prediction performance. Peer review includes C88 in their SUPPORTED evaluation (R9), affirming the value of 'combining expert opinion with model outputs' without expressing the same concerns about lack of specificity.

OpenEval evaluates combination approach (C88, C94) as UNCERTAIN due to limited concrete guidance. Peer review R10 addresses C94 as SUPPORTED, treating it as an established interpretive finding about how models and expert opinion could be combined, without raising concerns about lack of specificity.

Both evaluate model advantages (C91-C92) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the 4/5 months result and risk-ranking advantage are supported by data, though resource prioritization inference is not directly tested. Peer review accepts these findings without challenge as part of their broader interpretive conclusions.

OpenEval evaluates comparison to previous studies (C93) as UNCERTAIN, noting it's speculative since the study doesn't directly test time series vs. spatial forecasting by the same experts. Peer review includes C93 in their SUPPORTED evaluation (R10), treating it as an accepted interpretive finding without expressing concerns about the indirect nature of the comparison.

OpenEval evaluates interpretation of bias pattern (C73) as UNCERTAIN, noting it's speculative without direct evidence like expert interviews. No corresponding peer review evaluation found - peer reviewers did not separately assess this specific interpretation claim.
